newsitem.title: FRANCE: French parliament honours veteran Chaban-Delmas.
newsitem.headline: French parliament honours veteran Chaban-Delmas.

text.p: France's parliament paid tribute to former prime minister Jacques Chaban-Delmas on Tuesday, making him honorary Speaker of the National Assembly where he has been a member for 46 years, including 16 as chairman.
Chaban-Delmas, 81, once an international class rugby and tennis player and now virtually crippled after knee and hip surgery, had to be helped to the assembly microphone. He said he felt honoured.
The full house stood and applauded warmly when he thanked them for the appointment, made only once before in the parliament's 200-year odd history.
Serving Speaker Philippe Seguin said no one had served as long as Chaban-Delmas as assembly Speaker and only one man had served longer as member of parliament.
Chaban-Delmas will not be able to stand again for parliament. His own Rally for the Republic (RPR) party this month decided to set an age limit of 75 for candidates in the 1998 general election.

Chaban-Delmas' worst disappointment however came at the hands of Jacques Chirac, now France's president, who split the Gaullist party in half when he denied Chaban-Delmas his support and that of many Gaullists in the 1974 presidential election.

Chirac threw his support and that of many Gaullist parliamentarians behind centrist Valery Giscard d'Estaing who won the election and rewarded Chirac with the premiership before firing him two years later.
Chaban-Delmas had been prime minister under the late Georges Pompidou from 1969-1972 but was dumped because Pompidou found him too left-leaning.
Debonair and handsome - but with a high, nasal voice -- Chaban-Delmas was a World War Two Resistance hero and in 1944 became France's youngest brigadier general at the age of 29.
He was a good friend of late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand, a Resistance comrade-in-arms, and one of a very small group who addressed Mitterrand with the familiar "tu".

Chaban-Delmas' latest disappointment was last year when he was virtually forced to resign the Bordeaux town hall after being mayor there for 50 years to make room for Prime Minister Alain Juppe, a fellow Gaullist, who needed a new political base.
